target_customer: Gamers who pay for coaching, carries and boosting in games such as World of Warcraft, Call of Duty and Apex Legends; supply side is professional players paid per job
problem: Casual players want help with hard content or rank, and skilled players want paid work; there was no trusted, managed marketplace connecting them.
business_model: Marketplace take rate on coaching and carry orders, plus subscriptions

founders.name: Alex Beliankin
founders.background_notes: Former pro gamer once in the top 0.01% of World of Warcraft players per TechCrunch (2021-05-13). Named Aleksei Beliankin-Bauer on the YC page and Alexey Beliankin by VentureBeat. No co-founder is named in the sources read.

competitors.name: ProGuides
competitors.what: Los Angeles marketplace where gamers pay pros for sessions, about 25% commission
competitors.traction_then: Over 5,000 sessions in two months and about 250 coaches (August 2019)

competitors.name: Gamer Sensei
competitors.funding_then: About $6 million per Crunchbase as cited by TechCrunch

technical_complexity.rationale: A web marketplace with order management, payments and messaging bots; the hard parts are operations, vetting pros and support rather than software.

defensibility.rationale: Two-sided supply of vetted pros gives some network effect, but pros and buyers can multi-home and many boosting sites compete.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Game publishers restrict boosting in terms of service; esportslegal.news (2025-12) discusses the legality of WoW carry services. No publisher shutdown of LFcarry was found.

market_need_then: Founded 2016 and by September 2019 it had over 2,000 active players earning up to $5,000 per month (Kommersant via EWDN); demand for coaching and carries in WoW was already established.

branding.domain_note: Now lfcarry.com; the site footer links About us to /legionfarm. Domain change date not found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Claims such as #1 boosting and coaching service since 2016

rebrands.why: Not stated; YC page says formerly LegionFarm

branding.community_and_virality: About 10,000 Trustpilot reviews with a rating near 3.9 to 4.0 and mixed complaints about payments (Trustpilot, unverified).

brand_strength.rationale: Large review volume shows awareness among boosting customers, but the category carries a negative reputation, reviews include unverified fraud and unpaid staff complaints, and the name is niche.

pivots.to: Coaching subscriptions and hardware program for pros
pivots.why: TechCrunch 2021-05-13 says the company started a la carte and added subscriptions and a pro gear installment program

outcome_analysis: LegionFarm, now LFcarry, was founded in 2016, raised $1.5M in 2019, joined YC W20, then raised $6M in 2021 and an $11M extension in March 2022 despite Ukraine war disruption. It reports 525,000 completed orders and a team of 3 on YC. It looks like a durable but modest marketplace in a legally gray category; no later institutional rounds were found.
notes: VentureBeat says $17 million across the 2021 and 2022 rounds; the YC description says $17.8M from 20+ investors; aggregators list $19.58M or $22.75M and an unverified Series B and April 2020 $4M seed. The 2022 extension is labeled other because VentureBeat calls it additional funding. A Trustpilot reviewer alleged a TMT Investments fraud suit and unpaid former staff; neither was verified. Competitor dates are 2019, before the batch. Boosting-specific rivals (for example other WoW boosting sites) were not found in dated sources.
